cards.definition: A person or thing that does the action named by the word it follows.
Having or showing the quality named by the word it follows.
Without the thing or quality named by the word it follows.
The state or quality of being a certain way.
A very small amount compared with what is needed or with what is already there.
To officially put an end to a rule or practice.
Made with shapes, lines, or colors without showing things exactly as they look in real life.
A place with a service or business where information about one person or group is kept.
The nut of an oak tree. An acorn has a hard shell and a little cap.
A feature passed down in a group of living things that helps them survive or have young in a particular place.
Earth mixed with water and sometimes plant material, then formed into bricks or walls and allowed to dry.
A message designed to get people interested in a product, service, or idea.
A movable part near the outer end of an airplane wing that helps tip the plane to one side.
How hard the air pushes on something. It usually gets lower as you go higher above sea level.
A set of clear steps for solving a problem or doing a job.
One of the versions of DNA that can occur at a particular place.
Repeating the same starting sound in nearby words.
A material containing a metal mixed with one or more other elements.
The set of letters used to write one or more languages. The letters usually have an agreed order.
Words that describe what matters about an image for someone who cannot see it.
The height of a place or object compared with sea level or another starting level.
One of the tiny air sacs in the lungs where gases move between air and blood.
A change or addition made to a formal document, a law, or a proposal.
One of the small pieces a living body can join together to make a protein.
A large round or oval performance space with rows of seats around an open middle.
A clock that shows the time with hands that move around a face.
The amount of turn or opening between two lines or directions that meet.
Making pictures or objects seem to move by showing a series of slightly different images in order.
A system of laws that separated people by race in South Africa and gave most political power to white people.
A channel or pipe built to carry water from one place to another, sometimes across a bridge.
A layer of material under the ground that holds water and lets enough move through to supply a well or spring.
A curved structure that spans an opening and helps hold up what is above it.
A scientist who studies the people of the past through things they left behind, such as tools, buildings, or pieces of pottery.
A group or chain of islands. It can also mean the area of water that holds them.
A collection of records saved so people can consult them in the future, or the place that keeps them.
The amount of flat space inside a shape.
An agreement by people or countries fighting a war to stop the fighting.
A group arranged in rows and columns or another orderly pattern.
A tube that carries blood away from the heart.
A small, mostly rocky object that circles the Sun. Many of them travel between Mars and Jupiter.
The layer of gases held around a planet, moon, or star by gravity.
A tiny piece of matter that is still one particular chemical element. Gold is made of gold atoms, for example.
A glow in a planet’s upper atmosphere caused by particles giving energy to a gas there.
An imaginary or real line around which something turns.
A rod on which a wheel turns or that turns with a wheel.
One of the first teeth that grow in, most often later replaced with another tooth.
The part of a view or picture that seems farthest behind the main things in it.
An extra copy kept in case you lose the one you use.
A tiny living thing made of one cell. Some help other living things, while others can cause illness.
Long strips in some whales’ mouths that work like a strainer to catch tiny food.
Small hard balls and the rings that guide them, allowing parts of a machine to roll past each other smoothly.
A tank that can hold water or air to change how a boat or submarine floats.
A paper or another tool that lists choices for an election and lets a voter mark a choice.
A drawing that uses bars of different lengths to compare amounts.
A machine-readable pattern that stands for numbers or other information.
To trade goods or work directly without using money.
One of the places a runner tries to reach safely in a game such as baseball.
Two pieces that fit together as one rung on the ladder shape of DNA.
A broad low area or the whole area where water drains toward the same place.
A flying mammal with wings made of thin skin stretched over long finger bones.
A short stick carried and passed in a relay, or a short stick a conductor uses to guide musicians.
A device that uses stored chemical energy to push electric charge around a circuit.
A regular pulse you can often tap along with in music.
A muscle at the front of your upper arm that helps bend your elbow.
A liquid made by the liver that helps the body digest fats.
A plan for a new law, written so lawmakers can talk about it and vote on it.
Using only two choices, like the digits 0 and 1 in computer numbers.
A way to look in a sorted list by checking the middle and deciding which half to keep looking in.
Light made by a living thing using a process inside its body.
A small piece or amount of something.
A stretchy pouch inside the body that holds urine until you pee.
A tube inside an animal that carries blood.
A thick layer of fat under the skin that helps keep some ocean mammals warm.
An area of land that stays very wet, where partly decayed plants build up in the ground.
The temperature at which a liquid starts boiling at a particular pressure.
Soft tissue inside certain bones. One kind makes new blood cells.
Having to do with the two values true and false, or rules that use those values.
A line that shows where one area ends and another begins.
A long tool strung with hair or another fiber, drawn across strings to play a violin or a related instrument.
An organized refusal to buy, use, or take part in something in order to protest.
A little salty, as water can be where a river mixes with the sea.
A way to read and write using patterns of raised dots that can be felt with the fingers.
The organ inside your head that takes in signals and helps control the body.
The outer layers of a grain that may be taken off when it is milled.
An instrument played by buzzing into a mouthpiece, such as a trumpet or trombone.
To help people feel more comfortable and start talking when they first meet or feel shy.
To carry or guide someone or something to a place or to another person.
An app that requests and shows web pages.
An error in software or computer equipment that makes it work differently from how it should.
A short plant stem with thick layers that store food, often found underground.
The upward push that a liquid or gas gives to something in it.
An underground passage or home made or used by an animal.
To get something by paying money for it.
A group of eight bits that a computer handles as a unit.
A place that keeps a copy of information so a computer may use it again quickly.
An element that is part of strong bones and teeth and helps nerves and muscles do their jobs.
Lettering written with care as a form of art.
The breaking away of ice from the edge of a glacier to form floating pieces.
Color, shape, or pattern that makes a living thing hard to see in a place.
A waterway made by people to carry boats or to move water.
A device that stores energy by keeping opposite electric charges apart.
A tiny tube where materials can pass between blood and nearby tissue.
The city or town where a country’s or state’s main government is based.
Written words that help explain a picture or tell what you would hear in a video.
A hard covering over all or part of an animal’s back.
A group of travelers who make part of a trip together, often carrying goods.
A type of material that includes sugars, starches, and many kinds of fiber.
A gas whose molecules each contain one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms. You release some of it when you breathe out.
Adapted to get food or nutrients by eating animals.
A tough, bendy body material found in places such as your ears and joints.
To stop and hold something that is moving through the air or trying to get away.
A hollow space or, in a tooth, a hole caused by decay.
A tiny unit that can carry out the basic jobs of life. Living things are made of one or more cells.
A thin layer around a cell that helps control what goes in and out.
An official count of the people who live in a place. The count may also collect other information about them.
The point that describes where an object’s mass is balanced. It may fall in an empty space within the object.
A hard material, such as fired clay, usually made from minerals and set by heat.
A room or an enclosed space inside something.
A person, animal, or other being who takes part in a story.
To ask someone to pay a price for something.
An official document that sets out what a group is for and how it will work.
In chess, a position in which the king is under attack and no legal move can make it safe.
A change in which substances turn into other substances as atoms rearrange.
Making food using energy from chemicals instead of energy from sunlight.
A young person who has not yet grown into an adult.
A raised garden made from mud, plants, and other materials in shallow water, with canals around it.
A green substance in plants and some other living things that absorbs light used to make sugars.
To decide which person, thing, or action you want.
A group of different notes played or heard together as one musical unit.
A long piece of DNA and the proteins that help it fit inside a cell.
A path that electric charge can move through when the path makes a complete loop.
A device that opens part of a circuit automatically when more current flows than it is made to carry.
Movement around a place or along a path that brings something back again.
The distance around a circle.
A city and the land around it that have their own government.
A large society with a shared way of life and organized systems, often including cities, trade, or government.
The usual pattern of weather in a place over many years.
A lump that forms when pieces and materials in blood stick together.
One of the separate parts packed together in a garlic bulb.
A curled part of the inner ear that helps change sound vibrations into signals the brain can use.
An artwork made by attaching pieces of paper, cloth, or other material to a surface.
A place controlled by another country, often after people from that country settle there.
The way light makes something look red, blue, green, or another shade.
An icy object that travels around the Sun and can grow glowing tails of gas and dust as it warms up.
To look at two or more things to see how they are alike or different.
A person who creates a piece of music.
A dark mixture formed after scraps from plants and other living things break down.
A substance made of atoms from at least two different elements chemically joined in a fixed proportion.
A way to store or send information in less space than it took before.
The change from a gas to a liquid. It can happen when water vapor touches something cooler.
Something that has to be true for a rule or action to apply.
In a program, instructions that are used only if a particular test has the right result.
The movement of heat or electricity through something, such as through a metal spoon.
A material that lets electricity or heat move through it easily.
A solid shape with a round or other closed base and sides that narrow to a single point.
A cell in the eye that helps you see colors and details in enough light.
The basic rules that describe how a government is organized and what it can do. A constitution can also protect people’s rights.
One of the largest land areas into which people divide Earth. Different maps sometimes group them in different ways.
The way a gas or liquid carries heat as it moves from place to place.
One of the numbers that describes the position of a point on a map or grid.
A small ocean animal with a soft, tube-shaped body. Many corals live in groups and make hard structures that can build up into reefs.
Damage to a material after it reacts with substances around it, such as air or moisture.
A weight used to balance another weight or make it easier to move around.
A round hollow, often made where something struck a surface or around the opening of a volcano.
A marked line on a cricket pitch used to show a position or boundary in play.
A gradual increase in loudness in music.
Growing different kinds of crops on the same land in a planned order, often to keep soil healthy and reduce pests.
A solid with particles arranged in a pattern that repeats throughout it.
The space taken up by a cube whose edges are all one unit long.
Broken or crushed glass gathered for use when making new glass.
A soft lump of milk solids that can form when milk proteins gather together.
Wanting to know or find out about something.
The kind of money used in a country or shared by several countries.
A flow of water or air in a particular direction.
Using digital devices or online services to bully someone, such as by sending cruel or embarrassing messages.
A shape with two matching flat ends that are parallel, like the round ends of a can, joined by a side surface.
Information such as measurements, counts, or answers gathered to help you learn about something.
An organized set of information that a program can search and use.
To find and fix problems in a program or another system.
Describes a tree or shrub that drops most of its leaves for part of each year.
The dot that separates the ones place from the smaller places in a number.
A living thing that breaks dead material into simpler substances.
A hoofed animal with long legs. In many kinds, the males grow pointed, branching antlers each year.
A unit used to measure an angle or a temperature.
An area of land built from sand, mud, or other material dropped by a river near its mouth.
The bottom number in a fraction, showing how many equal parts make one whole.
How much matter is packed into a given amount of space. A small block of metal is usually denser than a wooden block of the same size.
The ability to notice how far away things are or which objects are nearer than others.
A feature that asks for proof that you are allowed to use a device before it opens.
The temperature to which air must cool before water vapor begins to turn into drops, if the amount of water in the air stays the same.
Going at a slant, like a line from one corner of a square to the opposite corner.
A way a group of people uses a language. It can have its own sounds, words, and ways of putting words together.
Words spoken back and forth between people or characters.
A straight line passing through the center of a circle from one edge to the other, or the length of that line.
The broad muscle below your lungs that helps you breathe.
The way your body breaks food down into small parts it can take in and use.
One of the symbols used to write a number, such as 0, 1, or 2.
To spread through another material in particles so small that you no longer see the separate pieces.
The long material carrying inherited information that many cells keep and use.
To act, work on a task, or carry it out.
A readable name used to identify a place or group of places on a network.
A round roof or ceiling that curves upward like part of a ball.
A small playing tile usually marked into two halves, each with a number of dots.
A fin that rises from the back of a swimming animal.
A graph that shows data by placing dots over the matching marks on a number line.
A force from a fluid such as air or water that opposes movement through it.
To make a picture, shape, or line by marking a surface.
To control a ball while moving, such as by bouncing it in basketball or with small kicks in soccer.
To take a liquid into your mouth and swallow it.
To control the movement of a car, truck, or other vehicle.
A hill or ridge of sand pushed together by wind or water.
An object that orbits the Sun, is nearly round, and shares its neighborhood with other objects of similar importance. It is not a moon.
How loud or soft sounds are in music and how the loudness changes.
A line of rulers from the same family, or the stretch of time when that family rules.
A thin layer of tissue in the ear that moves when sound reaches it.
A shaking of the ground that usually happens when rocks suddenly slip past one another deep below the surface.
To take food into your mouth and swallow it, usually after chewing.
A sound that returns after bouncing off a surface.
Finding where things are by making sounds and listening for the echoes that bounce back.
An event in space when one object blocks another from view or moves into its shadow.
The living things in a place, the nonliving things around them, and the ways they affect one another.
A line where two faces of a solid shape meet, or the outside of a flat shape.
How much time goes by between the start and end of an activity or event.
A substance that lets charged particles move through it, such as the substance between the ends of a battery.
A magnet that gets its magnetic field from flowing electricity.
A tiny part of matter with a negative electric charge. Electrons are found around the centers of atoms.
A basic chemical substance made of just one kind of atom, such as gold or oxygen.
A number of lands or peoples governed from one main center of power.
A mixture that holds tiny drops of one liquid spread through another liquid.
The hard outer coat on the part of a tooth above the gums.
Something that can be passed or stored and that makes changes possible, such as moving things, heating them, or making light.
A tiny biological helper that speeds up a change, such as breaking food into smaller pieces.
An imaginary line all the way around Earth halfway between the North Pole and South Pole.
Either of the two moments each year when Earth’s poles are tilted neither toward nor away from the Sun.
Equal in value or meaning, even if shown in a different way.
The wearing away and carrying off of soil or pieces of rock by moving water, wind, or ice, or by gravity.
The tube that carries swallowed food and drinks from the throat to the stomach.
To use clues to make a reasonable guess about a number, amount, or size.
A partly sheltered area near the coast where fresh water from land often mixes with salt water from the sea.
The change from liquid to gas that happens at a liquid’s surface.
A whole number that can be put into pairs with none left over.
The boundary around a black hole beyond which nothing can escape to the outside.
A plant that keeps some green leaves throughout the year.
Facts, objects, or observations that help you check whether an idea is true.
Change in the traits that living things pass to their young over many generations.
A planet outside our solar system.
A short story, often about animals that act like people, that suggests a lesson.
One flat surface of a solid shape.
A number that multiplies by another number to make a given number.
To move downward or drop, usually because of gravity.
A way of organizing a country so that power is divided between a national government and governments for smaller parts, such as states.
A way some living things get energy by changing sugars into other substances.
Parts of plant food that your own digestive juices break down only a little or not at all.
A thin thread of glass or plastic that carries light along it.
Stories about imagined characters or events, even when some details come from real life.
A named group of information kept on a computer.
A short ending after a dot in a filename, often used to show the type of file.
Something that lets some parts of a mixture through and holds other parts back.
A long, narrow arm of the sea between steep slopes, formed when seawater filled a valley carved by ice.
A flat limb that helps an animal swim or steer.
A fine powder made by grinding grain, beans, or similar foods. People use it in bread and many other foods.
The part of some plants that helps them make seeds. It often has colorful petals.
One of the broad sections of a whale’s two-part tail.
To move through the air, with wings, in an aircraft, or in another way.
A trip that takes a spacecraft close past an object so it can observe it.
An outer arch that carries a push from the upper part of a building out to a strong support on the ground.
A named place that holds files or other folders on a computer.
A traditional story people pass from one teller to another over time.
A tiny pocket in the body, such as the kind in skin where a hair begins.
A picture or idea showing who eats whom among many living things in one place.
The part of a person’s or animal’s body at the end of a leg that touches the ground when standing or walking.
A push or pull that can change how something moves or change its shape.
The part of a picture that seems closest to the viewer.
To stop remembering something or fail to think of it when you need it.
The shape of something, especially its shape in three dimensions.
A part, shape, or trace of a living thing from long ago that was preserved naturally.
A way to name a number by telling how many equal parts of a whole you have.
Easy to break or damage, so it needs careful handling.
One picture in a series that makes a film or animation.
Poetry that can use flexible line lengths without a required pattern of beats or rhymes.
To change from a liquid to a solid because of cold, or make that happen.
The temperature at which a liquid forms solid crystals under given conditions.
One of the thin bars across the neck of a guitar or similar instrument, used to guide where a string stops vibrating.
A force that acts between touching surfaces to resist sliding, or that can stop them from starting to slide.
The part that develops from a flowering plant’s ovary and usually contains seeds.
The point that a lever turns around.
In programming, a group of steps a program can use as one unit, often by calling it by name.
A living thing such as a mushroom, mold or yeast that gets food by absorbing it from other material.
An enormous group of stars, gas, and dust held together by gravity.
A small pouch under the liver that stores some bile.
A kind of matter that spreads out to fill the space around it. Air is a mixture of several gases.
A toothed wheel that moves another toothed part and can change speed, force or direction.
A stretch of DNA whose information a cell can use for a particular job.
A machine that makes electricity, often by spinning wires or magnets.
All the inherited information in a living thing.
A scientist who studies rocks and what they show about a world’s past.
Energy supplied by heat from inside Earth.
To start growing from a seed or spore.
A hot spring that sometimes shoots water and steam out of the ground.
To pass something to someone so they can use it, keep it, or have it for a while.
A huge mass of ice that forms on land as layers of snow pile up and squeeze together. It moves slowly under its own weight.
A coating that can become glassy when heated on pottery.
A carved, drawn, or printed sign that represents something, such as a sound, word, or number.
To move or travel from one place to another.
A large waterbird with a long neck and feet that help it paddle.
To join a piece cut from one plant to a part of another plant so that they grow together.
A small hard seed or fruit from a crop such as corn, wheat, oats or rice.
A soft form of carbon in which flat layers of atoms can slip past one another.
Plant growth that changes direction in response to gravity.
The attraction between things that have mass. It pulls objects toward Earth and holds planets in their paths around the Sun.
A pattern of lines that makes rows and columns.
Water found below the surface in gaps in soil and rock.
To get bigger or develop over time, or to make a plant develop by taking care of it.
A short kind of poem that began in Japan and often notices a brief moment in nature.
To keep trying or wait patiently when something is hard or slow.
An area of deep enough water where boats can stay with some shelter from wind and waves.
The physical parts of a computer or other device that you could touch.
Two or more notes sounding together, or the way groups of notes fit with a tune.
To notice sounds with your ears.
Energy that moves from a warmer object or place to a cooler one because of that difference in temperature.
The distance from the bottom of something to its top, or how tall a person or object is.
One half of a ball-shaped object, especially one half of Earth.
A material in red blood cells that can pick up oxygen and let it go again.
An animal that eats mainly or only plants.
In or to the place where you are or where you are pointing.
To put yourself or something else where it cannot easily be seen or found.
One sign in a writing system that uses picture-like shapes to stand for sounds, words, or ideas. Ancient Egyptians used such signs.
An area of land that stands high above the country around it.
To begin studying, especially with care and effort.
To have something in your hand, arms, or another secure place.
An opening through a thing, or a space that goes into a surface.
One of two or more words that sound the same but have different meanings, such as sea and see.
A chemical message made in your body that changes what some cells do.
How well the body has enough water to do its jobs.
The use of a liquid under pressure to move things or apply a force.
The lightest chemical element, made of atoms whose centers have one proton. It is found in water and in stars.
A place on the sea floor where hot water from below comes out through an opening.
One of two babies who began from the same fertilized egg and usually have very similar DNA.
A group of words that means something different as a group from what the separate words might suggest.
Rock made when melted material cools and becomes solid.
A drawing or picture that shows something from a story or helps explain a subject.
The amount of picture detail a grid can store, often described by how many pixels it has across and down.
A person who comes to live in another country.
Making up part of a performance as you do it.
Something you pay for from inside a game or other app.
A front tooth with a sharp edge used for cutting into food.
An organized set of clues that helps someone or something find information quickly.
In chemistry, a substance that shows something about a liquid, often by changing color.
A kind of light that human eyes cannot see. Warm things often give off infrared light.
To get a feature or piece of genetic information from biological parents.
The part of the ear farthest from the outside that contains organs for hearing and balance.
One part of a baseball game in which each team has a turn to bat.
A number, fact, or signal you give to a rule, device, or system.
Words or signs written, stamped, or cut onto a surface, such as stone, metal, or paper.
The worldwide system that connects many networks and lets computers exchange information.
A long, folded tube in the body that helps take useful parts from food and carry along the rest.
The colored ring in an eye that changes the size of the opening in its center.
An element that can be a metal and is also needed in tiny forms by the body to help carry oxygen.
Bringing water to land or plants with pipes, channels, or other equipment, especially when rain alone is not enough.
A narrow strip of land that joins two larger areas of land, with water on both sides.
A narrow band of fast-moving air high in the sky.
A puzzle made of pieces whose edges fit together, usually forming a picture when all the pieces are in place.
A place where bones meet.
A group chosen to hear information and make a decision in a court case.
To watch someone or something and be ready to notice a change or problem.
A kind of large brown seaweed.
A tough material your body makes for parts such as hair, nails, and the outer layer of skin.
One of the body parts that clean the blood and make urine from some waste and extra water.
An oven that gets very hot, used for heating clay pots and other materials.
In earlier times in parts of Europe, a trained warrior who often rode a horse and served a ruler. In some places today, knighthood is a special honor.
To have learned or understood something so that you can remember or use it.
Small swimming animals with bodies shaped a little like tiny shrimp.
A shallow body of water separated from a larger body of water by a strip of land or a reef.
Surrounded by land with no coast on the open ocean.
A measure in degrees of how far north or south a place is from the equator.
Melted rock that reaches Earth’s surface, or the rock it makes after cooling.
To guide people or animals by showing them where to go or what to do.
A small passage in a leaf that carries water or sugars through it.
To go away from a place or person.
A small electronic part that gives off light when electricity flows through it in the proper direction.
The group of people responsible for making laws for a country, state, or other area.
A plant in the pea family or a food seed from such a plant.
A stiff bar that turns around a point and helps move something.
A place or service where people can read, borrow, or use shared books and other materials.
A partnership in which a fungus grows with an alga or a tiny organism that can make sugars from light.
A force, often from moving air, that acts across the direction of motion and can hold an aircraft up.
A strong band of body tissue that helps join bones and guide motion at a joint.
A kind of energy that lets our eyes see things when it reaches them.
The distance light can travel in one year, about 9.5 trillion kilometers.
A kind of rock made mostly of calcium carbonate, the material in many shells and corals.
Something that connects two things, such as a ring in a chain or an item on a page that opens another page.
A kind of matter that flows and takes the shape of the part of a container it fills.
An organ that sorts and changes some things brought by the blood and makes a liquid that helps digest fats.
Something being carried, lifted, or supported.
A word that people speaking one language take from another language and start using.
A measure in degrees of how far east or west a place is from a line called the prime meridian.
A long, narrow boat that people used in the Viking Age, with a sail and places for oars.
A tool or frame that holds threads steady for weaving.
In programming, a group of steps that can run repeatedly.
To stop having something or be unable to find it.
Hot, partly or fully melted rock beneath Earth’s surface.
An object that can attract certain metals, such as iron, and pull or push other magnets without touching them.
The angle between the direction a compass points locally and the direction to Earth’s geographic north pole.
The area in which a magnet or moving electric charge can exert a magnetic force.
To create or put something together.
A kind of animal whose mothers feed their young milk. Mammals have hair at least at some stage in life.
A family of games in which players move small counters one at a time among pits on a board.
A measure of how much matter something contains or how hard it is to change its motion.
An average found by adding numbers and dividing the total by how many numbers you added.
The middle value in an ordered list, or the value halfway between the two middle numbers when there are two.
To come together with someone, whether you planned it or not. It can also mean being introduced for the first time.
The line of notes that makes the main tune of a piece of music.
Information that describes a file or other piece of information.
Rock changed from an older rock by heat, pressure, or other changes inside Earth, without melting completely.
A comparison that talks about one thing as though it were something else.
A streak of light made when a small object speeds through a planet’s atmosphere.
A piece of rock or metal from space that reaches the ground after traveling through an atmosphere.
A gas that contains carbon and hydrogen. In cold places such as Titan it can form liquid lakes.
A system of measurements with units such as the meter, liter, and gram, related by powers of ten.
A condition in which objects act as if there is very little gravity pulling them against their surroundings.
A solid material that forms in nature and has its own chemical makeup and a regular pattern inside.
Wrongly or in a way that makes a mistake.
A small cell part that helps make energy from food available for the cell to use.
A way a cell sorts copies of its chromosomes into two groups before it splits into two cells.
Two or more kinds of material together that can still keep their own properties.
A large tooth farther back in the mouth, used to crush and grind food.
A group of two or more atoms held together by chemical bonds.
A wind pattern that changes direction with the seasons and often brings a rainy season.
A natural object that travels around a planet, dwarf planet, or other small world. We call Earth’s own moon the Moon.
A ridge or pile of loose material carried and left by a glacier.
The lesson that a story asks you to think about.
A picture or pattern made by fitting together many small pieces of stone, tile, glass, or another material.
A machine that makes a part move using power from electricity, fuel or another source.
A small animal with sharp front teeth for gnawing, rounded ears, and usually a long tail.
A covering such as straw or wood chips laid over soil to help hold water or limit weeds.
A number made by multiplying a given number by a whole number.
A place or organization that collects, cares for, and shows objects or works so people can learn about them.
The spreading network of fine threads that makes up much of a fungus.
A close partnership where a fungus grows with a plant’s roots.
The voice or person that tells a story.
A legal process through which someone becomes a citizen of a country after birth.
An enormous cloud of gas, dust or both in space.
A number less than zero.
A tiny part of a kidney that filters the blood, then takes useful material back.
